stem: A toddler with suspected foreign body aspiration has unilateral overinflation on imaging; which mechanism best explains this finding?

options.text: Partial expiratory obstruction creates a ball-valve effect with air trapping and overinflation
Complete obstruction prevents all air entry and causes overinflation
Partial inspiratory obstruction allows the lung to empty normally
The opposite lung cannot ventilate, so the affected lung overinflates
The object is in the digestive tract rather than the airway

explanation: Partial expiratory obstruction creates a ball-valve effect. In foreign body aspiration, air can enter the airway during inspiration but cannot escape well during expiration, leading to air trapping and unilateral overinflation.

citations.source: Louisa Leone MD3 2025 - Child and Adolescent Health - Study Notes.pdf
citations.title: Louisa Leone MD3 2025 - Child and Adolescent Health - Study Notes.pdf p.142

optionExplanations.A: Correct because partial expiratory obstruction allows inspiratory air entry but impairs expiration, producing a ball-valve effect with air trapping and overinflation.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect because complete obstruction would block air entry and exit rather than cause air trapping with overinflation.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect because the key mechanism is impaired expiration, not isolated inspiratory obstruction with normal emptying.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect because unilateral overinflation is caused by the affected airway’s ball-valve effect, not failure of the opposite lung.
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect because this pattern is due to airway foreign body aspiration, not a digestive tract object.

sourceRefs: Louisa Leone MD3 2025 - Child and Adolescent Health - Study Notes.pdf
